case_name: Cr. A. No. 214/2014 vs Ranjodh Singh & Ors
facts_of_case: The victim's marriage was solemnized with the accused/respondent No.1 Ranjodh Singh. The accused persons started harassing the victim and demanded dowry from her. The victim told her mother and brothers about the harassment, but the matter was not settled.

legal_principles.principle: The acquittal of the accused further strengthens the presumption of innocence;
legal_principles.held: The principles which govern the exercise of appellate jurisdiction while dealing with an appeal against acquittal under Section 378 of Cr.P.C. can be summarised as follows: -

legal_principles.principle: The Appellate Court, while hearing an appeal against acquittal, is entitled to re-appreciate the oral and documentary evidence;
legal_principles.held: The principles which govern the exercise of appellate jurisdiction while dealing with an appeal against acquittal under Section 378 of Cr.P.C. can be summarised as follows: -

legal_principles.principle: The Appellate Court, while deciding an appeal against acquittal, after re-appreciating the evidence, is required to consider whether the view taken by the Trial Court is a possible view which could have been taken on the basis of the evidence on record;
legal_principles.held: The principles which govern the exercise of appellate jurisdiction while dealing with an appeal against acquittal under Section 378 of Cr.P.C. can be summarised as follows: -

legal_principles.principle: If the view taken is a possible view, the Appellate Court cannot overturn the order of acquittal on the ground that another view was also possible;
legal_principles.held: The principles which govern the exercise of appellate jurisdiction while dealing with an appeal against acquittal under Section 378 of Cr.P.C. can be summarised as follows: -

legal_principles.principle: The Appellate Court can interfere with the order of acquittal only if it comes to a finding that the only conclusion which can be recorded on the basis of the evidence on record was that the guilt of the accused was proved beyond a reasonable doubt and no other conclusion was possible;
